Anyone looking at him might have thought that Nemesis, the goddess of vengeance, had stolen Pallas’s shield and shown him the Gorgon’s head. He seemed frozen into stone, his sorrowful face as still as marble. He had enjoyed the refined, luxurious life of a young man with wealth and good family: a beautiful life free of money worries, full of carefree boyish pleasure. Now, for the first time, he understood something of Destiny’s terrible mystery and the dreadful meaning of Doom.

How mad and monstrous it all seemed! Could his hand contain some awful secret of sin, some blood-red mark of crime, written in signs he could not read but someone else understood? Was there no way to escape? Were people merely chess pieces moved by an invisible force, or pots that a potter shaped as he pleased, for honourable or shameful uses? His reason rebelled, yet he felt a tragedy looming over him. Suddenly he had been given a burden too heavy to bear. How lucky actors were. They could choose between tragedy and comedy, between suffering and pleasure, between laughter and tears. Real life offered no such choice. Most men and women were forced into roles they were not suited to play. Our Guildensterns had to act as Hamlet, while our Hamlets must joke like Prince Hal. The world was a stage, but its actors had been assigned the wrong parts.

Suddenly Mr. Podgers came into the room. The sight of Lord Arthur made him start, and his heavy, coarse face turned a greenish yellow. Their eyes met. For a moment neither spoke.

‘The Duchess left a glove here, Lord Arthur, and asked me to fetch it,’ Mr. Podgers said at last. ‘Ah, there it is on the sofa! Good evening.’

‘Mr. Podgers, I insist that you give me an honest answer to the question I am about to ask.’

‘Another time, Lord Arthur. The Duchess is waiting anxiously. I’m afraid I must leave.’

‘You will stay. The Duchess is in no hurry.’

‘One shouldn’t keep ladies waiting, Lord Arthur,’ said Mr. Podgers with his weak, sickly smile. ‘Women are inclined to be impatient.’

Lord Arthur’s finely shaped lips curled with irritated contempt. At that moment the poor Duchess seemed of very little importance to him. He crossed the room to Mr. Podgers and held out his hand.

‘Tell me what you saw in it,’ he said. ‘Tell me the truth. I have to know. I am not a child.’

‘Shucks, Tom,’ I says, ‘seems like you could tell a body. What’s this bar sinister?’

‘Oh, I don’t know myself. But he’s bound to have one. Every nobleman does.’

That was Tom all over. When he didn’t feel like explaining something, there warn’t no making him. You could question him a whole week and never get any further.

He had that coat-of-arms affair settled now, so he went ahead with what remained of that piece of the business, which was inventing a sorrowful inscription. He said Jim must have one, the same as all the others. He thought up several and set them down on paper, and this is how he read them out:

Here broke the heart of a captive.

Here a wretched prisoner, abandoned by friends and the world, pined away his sorrowful days.

Here a solitary heart was broken, and a weary spirit found rest, following thirty-seven years of imprisonment alone.

Here died a noble stranger, the natural son of Louis XIV, without home or friends, after thirty-seven bitter years in captivity.

Tom read them with his voice shaking and came mighty near breaking down. Afterwards he couldn't decide which Jim ought to scratch on the wall, because every one was so fine. Finally he reckoned he’d allow him to put them all there. Jim said scratching that much stuff into the logs with a nail would take a year, and anyhow he didn’t know how to form letters. Tom said he’d mark them out first, so Jim would only need to follow along the lines. Pretty soon Tom says:

‘Now I think of it, them logs won’t answer. Dungeons don’t have walls made of logs. We’ve got to cut these inscriptions into a stone. We’ll bring a stone in.’

Jim said a stone was worse than the logs. It would take such a dreadful long while to cut everything into rock that he’d never get free. But Tom said he’d permit me to help with it. Then he looked over the pens to see what progress me and Jim was making. It was awful tedious, hard, slow work, and it never gave the sores on my hands any chance to heal. We hardly seemed to get ahead at all. So Tom says:

‘I know the way to manage it. We need a rock for that coat of arms and those sorrowful inscriptions, and we can kill two birds with the very same rock.’

He had, indeed, been entirely unaware of his own power over her. When he followed her into the shrubbery, he had no thought of putting it to the test. He had come out of concern to discover how she endured Frank Churchill’s engagement, with no interested purpose—no purpose whatever beyond offering comfort or advice, should she give him the opportunity. Everything else had sprung from the moment, from the immediate action upon his feelings of what she said. The joyful certainty that she was wholly indifferent to Frank Churchill, that her heart remained entirely unattached to him, had awakened a hope that he might eventually win her love himself. Yet he had expected nothing at present; only, in that brief victory of eagerness over prudence, he had ventured to desire assurance that she would not forbid his endeavour to gain her affection. The greater hopes that opened by degrees were therefore still more delightful. The love he had begged leave to inspire, if he were able, belonged to him already! In less than half an hour he had moved from deep unhappiness to a state so nearly perfect felicity that it deserved no other description.

Her alteration was no less great. That same half-hour had bestowed upon both the precious knowledge of being loved, and removed from each an equal measure of uncertainty, jealousy, or mistrust. His jealousy was of long duration, dating from Frank Churchill’s coming, or even from the anticipation of it. His love for Emma and his jealousy of Frank Churchill had begun at nearly the same time; probably one feeling had revealed the other to him. That jealousy had driven him away from the country. The excursion to Box Hill had determined his departure. He would spare himself another sight of attentions so openly permitted and encouraged. He went away to acquire indifference, but chose the wrong destination. His brother’s house contained too much domestic happiness; woman appeared there in too pleasing a shape. Isabella resembled Emma too closely, except in those conspicuous shortcomings that continually recalled the other’s brilliance, for him to have accomplished much, even with more time. Nevertheless he had persevered in staying, day after day, until that very morning’s post brought Jane Fairfax’s story. Then, accompanying the pleasure he could not avoid—and did not hesitate to feel, since he had never considered Frank Churchill worthy of Emma—came such tender concern, such sharp anxiety for her, that he could remain no longer. He had ridden home in the rain, and directly after dinner walked up to discover how this sweetest and best of creatures, faultless despite all her faults, was bearing the revelation.
